_readme: See README.md in this folder for source policy, field meanings and the Unverified list.

ingredients.season: Early to late summer, picked as the flowers open

culpeper.heading: CAMOMILE.
culpeper.quote: it is so well known every where, that it is but lost time and labour to describe it
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed a camomile bath eased weariness and aches. He names no ruling planet, but repeats the story that the Egyptians dedicated it to the Sun.

folklore.text: Gardeners once called chamomile the 'plant's physician', believing a drooping plant set beside it would revive. It was also strewn underfoot and planted in walks, where treading seemed to help it spread.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: NCCIH says studies have not produced enough reliable evidence to rate chamomile's usefulness for any condition; the little research on sleep found no benefit.

ingredients.safety: Likely safe as a tea. Can cause allergic reactions, especially with ragweed or daisy allergies. May interact with warfarin, sedatives and birth control pills.
ingredients.card: Gardeners once called chamomile the plant's physician, and swore a wilting neighbour perked up beside it. The Greeks thought it smelled like apples, so they named it the ground apple.
ingredients.true_fact: Chamomile's Spanish name, manzanilla, means 'little apple', after its apple-like scent.

ingredients.season: Midsummer: Culpeper says it flowers about the end of June and beginning of July

culpeper.heading: LAVENDER.
culpeper.quote: Mercury owns the herb; and it carries his effects very potently.
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed lavender, Mercury's herb, helped griefs of the head and brain from cold causes, but warned its fierce oil ('Oil of Spike') should be used only a few drops at a time.

folklore.text: Lavender was first recorded as cultivated in England around 1568. Dried flowers scented linen and were thought to keep moths away, and lavender was one of the old London street cries.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: NCCIH says a few small studies hint oral lavender oil might help anxiety, but the research has real limits; it is unclear whether lavender aromatherapy helps sleep, stress or pain.

ingredients.safety: Likely safe in food amounts. Skin products can cause allergic reactions. May add to the effects of sedatives. Little known about pregnancy safety.
ingredients.card: For centuries, lavender went into the linen press as much as the medicine chest: dried sprigs scented sheets and gloves and were thought to keep the moths away.
ingredients.true_fact: The name lavender may come from the Latin lavare, 'to wash', from its use in bathing.

ingredients.season: Summer: leaves at their best just before the plant flowers

culpeper.heading: MINT.
culpeper.quote: being once planted in a garden, will hardly be rid out again
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed mint, an herb of Venus, was very profitable to the stomach. He described spear mint, not peppermint, and warned that it spreads by its roots.

folklore.text: Peppermint was only recognised as a distinct plant late in the 17th century: John Ray described it in 1696. It entered the London Pharmacopoeia in 1721, and Mitcham farms grew it from about 1750.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: NCCIH says enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules may ease overall IBS symptoms in adults, but very little research exists on peppermint leaf or tea.

ingredients.safety: Tea appears safe. Oil can cause heartburn or skin irritation. Never put peppermint oil on an infant's or young child's face.
ingredients.card: Peppermint is a newcomer to the herb garden: it was only described as its own plant in the late 1600s. Like all mints, once it moves into a bed, it rarely leaves.
ingredients.true_fact: Peppermint is a natural hybrid of water mint and spearmint.

ingredients.season: Early summer until the first frosts

culpeper.heading: MARIGOLDS.
culpeper.quote: It is an herb of the Sun, and under Leo.
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed marigolds, ruled by the Sun, strengthened the heart, and noted the flowers were much used in possets, broths and drinks to comfort the heart and spirits.

folklore.text: In 1699 a writer reported Dutch grocers keeping whole barrels of dried marigold petals for winter broths, sold by the penny. The flowers were also once used to colour cheese yellow.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) accept calendula only as a traditional herbal product for minor skin and mouth inflammation, based on long use; clinical studies were too flawed to draw firm conclusions.

ingredients.safety: Can cause skin allergy. Avoid with daisy-family (Asteraceae) allergies. Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding not established.
ingredients.card: Dutch grocers once kept barrels of dried marigold petals by the counter, and folk said no good winter broth was made without a pinch. Sunny petals, sunny soup.
ingredients.true_fact: Calendula is named from the Latin calendae, the first day of the month: it was said to bloom every month.

ingredients.season: Evergreen: leaves all year; flowers in spring

culpeper.heading: ROSEMARY.
culpeper.quote: The Sun claims privilege in it, and it is under the celestial Ram.
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed rosemary, the Sun's herb, warmed all cold diseases of the head and stomach and 'helps a weak memory'. He valued it for civil as well as physical uses.

folklore.text: Rosemary was the herb of remembrance and fidelity: brides wore sprigs in their wreaths, wedding guests received gilded branches, and mourners dropped sprigs onto coffins.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) list rosemary leaf only as a traditional herbal product for mild indigestion and minor muscle aches, based on long-standing use rather than clinical studies.

ingredients.safety: Safe as a kitchen herb. Medicinal use not advised in pregnancy, breastfeeding, gallstones or liver disease. Can cause contact dermatitis.
ingredients.card: Rosemary is for remembrance. Brides wove it into their wreaths, guests carried gilded sprigs home from weddings, and mourners laid it on coffins so no one would be forgotten.
ingredients.true_fact: Botanists now place rosemary in the sage genus: its accepted name is Salvia rosmarinus.

ingredients.season: Late spring to midsummer, before and as it flowers

culpeper.heading: SAGE.
culpeper.quote: Jupiter claims this, and bids me tell you
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed sage, ruled by Jupiter, was good for the liver and blood, and repeated older writers praising it for pains in the head and joints.

folklore.text: An old Latin saying asks why anyone should die while sage grows in the garden. Another belief held that a sage plant thrives or withers along with its owner's fortunes.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: NCCIH says only small amounts of research exist; a few small studies suggest common sage might reduce menopausal hot flashes, but no firm conclusions can be drawn.

ingredients.safety: Safe in food amounts. Contains thujone, which can be toxic in large amounts or long use. May be unsafe in pregnancy.
ingredients.card: An old Latin proverb asks: why should anyone die while sage grows in the garden? Folk also said a sage bush flourishes when its household does, and droops when it doesn't.
ingredients.true_fact: Sage's genus name, Salvia, comes from the Latin salvere, 'to be saved' or 'to be well'.

ingredients.season: Early summer, as it begins to flower; leaves usable most of the year

culpeper.heading: THYME.
culpeper.quote: It is in vain to describe an herb so commonly known.
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed thyme, 'a notable herb of Venus', was a noble strengthener of the lungs and comforted the stomach.

folklore.text: Thyme stood for courage. In the age of chivalry, ladies embroidered a bee hovering over a sprig of thyme on the scarves they gave their knights.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) accept thyme only as a traditional herbal product for chesty coughs with colds; the clinical studies they reviewed were too small for firm conclusions.

ingredients.safety: Safe as a kitchen herb. Avoid with mint-family (Lamiaceae) allergies. Can upset the stomach. Medicinal use not advised in pregnancy.
ingredients.card: Thyme meant courage. Knights rode off wearing scarves embroidered with a bee above a sprig of thyme, and Greek honey from the thyme-covered hills was famous.
ingredients.true_fact: The honey of Mount Hymettus near Athens was famed in ancient times; its flavour was credited to wild thyme.

ingredients.season: Late spring to midsummer, before it flowers

culpeper.heading: BALM.
culpeper.quote: it causes the mind and heart to become merry
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed balm, an herb of Jupiter under Cancer, strengthened nature, and quoted Arabian physicians who said it drove away troublesome cares and melancholy.

folklore.text: Beekeepers rubbed hives with balm leaves, believing it kept their bees together and drew in new swarms. Pliny wrote that straying bees found their way home by it.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) accept lemon balm only as a traditional herbal product for mild stress, sleep and digestive upsets; the one small trial they reviewed was too flawed for firm conclusions.

ingredients.safety: May cause drowsiness; avoid driving if affected. Not established for children under 12, pregnancy or breastfeeding.
ingredients.card: Melissa means 'bee' in Greek, and bees adore this lemony herb. Old beekeepers rubbed their hives with the leaves so their swarms would always find their way home.
ingredients.true_fact: Lemon balm's botanical name, Melissa, is the Greek word for 'bee'.

ingredients.season: Flowers in early summer; berries ripen in late summer to early autumn

culpeper.heading: THE ELDER TREE.
culpeper.quote: every boy that plays with a pop-gun will not mistake another tree instead of Elder
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed elder, under Venus, carried off phlegm and choler. He thought it so well known that any boy with an elder pop-gun could name it.

folklore.text: Danish folklore told of the Hylde-Moer, an Elder Mother spirit living in the tree. Woodcutters asked her permission before cutting, and furniture made of elder wood was said to be haunted.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: NCCIH says some preliminary research suggests elderberry may relieve cold and flu symptoms, but there is not enough information on other uses; no good evidence supports COVID-19 claims.

ingredients.safety: Raw or unripe berries, leaves and stems are poisonous (cyanide-producing), causing vomiting and diarrhoea. Only cooked ripe berries are eaten.
ingredients.card: In Danish folklore an Elder Mother lived in the tree, and you asked her leave before taking a branch. Its berries make fine jam, but only ripe and cooked: raw, they make you ill.
ingredients.true_fact: Raw elderberries, leaves and stems contain cyanide-producing substances; cooking the ripe berries removes them.

ingredients.season: Summer into early autumn

culpeper.heading: YARROW, CALLED NOSE-BLEED, MILFOIL AND THOUSAND-LEAL.
culpeper.quote: Achilles is supposed to be the first that left the virtues of this herb to posterity
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed yarrow, an herb of Dame Venus, was drying and binding, and fit for ointments for wounds. He credited Achilles with first recording its virtues.

folklore.text: Folk sewed yarrow into flannel and slept on it while reciting a verse, hoping to dream of a future spouse. In Sweden it was called Field Hop and brewed into beer.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) accept yarrow only as a traditional herbal product for appetite loss, mild digestive upsets, period cramps and small wounds, based on long use, not clinical trials.

ingredients.safety: Can cause allergic skin reactions. Avoid with daisy-family (Asteraceae) allergies.
ingredients.card: Legend says Achilles took yarrow to war with him, which is how it got its name, Achillea. Lovesick folk slept with it under their pillows to dream of their sweethearts.
ingredients.true_fact: Yarrow's genus, Achillea, is named after the Greek hero Achilles.

ingredients.season: Late summer to autumn, when the seeds ripen

culpeper.heading: FENNEL.
culpeper.quote: One good old fashion is not yet left off, viz. to boil Fennel with fish
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed fennel, an herb of Mercury under Virgo, was good to break wind, and that cooking it with fish worked because Virgo opposes Pisces.

folklore.text: In the Middle Ages fennel was hung over doors on Midsummer's Eve to keep evil spirits away. On fast days the poor ate it to quiet hunger and liven plain food.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) accept sweet fennel fruit only as a traditional herbal product for mild bloating, period cramps and chesty coughs, based on long use rather than clinical evidence.

ingredients.safety: Generally well tolerated; can cause skin or breathing allergies, especially with celery- or dill-family or mugwort allergies. Medicinal use not advised in pregnancy.
ingredients.card: On Midsummer's Eve, medieval households hung fennel over their doors to keep mischief out. Cooks have paired its anise-sweet seeds with fish for centuries.
ingredients.true_fact: Charlemagne ordered fennel grown on his imperial farms, helping it spread through central Europe.

ingredients.season: Tropical: in a northern garden only under glass, lifted in autumn

folklore.text: In medieval Europe ginger was a costly import carried along long, taxed trade routes. Noble households perfumed great halls with spiced wine fountains that included ginger.
folklore.source: Newberry Library, 'The Medieval Spice Trade' (Digital Collections for the Classroom)

science.text: NCCIH says research suggests ginger may help nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and possibly period cramps; most studies of motion sickness have not shown benefit.

ingredients.safety: Can cause heartburn, stomach discomfort or mouth irritation. Ask a health provider before using supplements in pregnancy or alongside medicines.
ingredients.card: Ginger came to medieval Europe from far-off Asia along long, costly trade roads, so precious that great halls bubbled with spiced-wine fountains just to show it off.
ingredients.true_fact: The ginger we cook with is a rhizome, an underground stem, not a true root.

ingredients.season: Early summer, when the once-blooming old roses flower

culpeper.heading: ROSES.
culpeper.quote: What a pother have authors made with Roses! What a racket have they kept?
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed red roses were under Jupiter, damask under Venus and white under the Moon, and that roses were cooling and drying, binding more when dried.

folklore.text: A rose hung over the dinner table once meant everything said there was secret: 'sub rosa'. The plaster ornament in the middle of a ceiling is still called a rose.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) accept rose petals only as a traditional herbal product for mild mouth, throat and skin inflammation; one small mouthwash study was promising but not enough on its own.

ingredients.safety: No side effects known from EU review. Medicinal use not established for children under 12 or in pregnancy.
ingredients.card: A rose hung above the table meant 'what's said here stays here', which is why secrets are told sub rosa. Apothecaries once pounded the red petals with sugar into a sweet conserve.
ingredients.true_fact: Rose hips are the rose's fruit. In 1941, British volunteers and schoolchildren gathered 200 tons of them to make vitamin C syrup when oranges were scarce.

ingredients.season: Spring, when the young tops are tender

culpeper.heading: NETTLES.
culpeper.quote: they may be found by feeling, in the darkest night
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed nettles, hot and dry under Mars, eaten as spring tops cleared away winter's cold, moist humours.

folklore.text: Nettle fibre was woven into household linen in 16th and 17th century Scotland. During the First World War, cotton was scarce in Germany, and its army turned to nettle fibre for cloth.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) accept nettle leaf only as a traditional herbal product for minor joint pain and to increase urine flow, based on long-standing use rather than clinical trials.

ingredients.safety: Fresh plants sting the skin. Can cause mild stomach upset or rash. Medicinal use not advised in pregnancy, or with heart or kidney disease.
ingredients.card: Nettles sting, but they also clothe and feed. Scottish homes once wove nettle linen, and spring nettle soup is an old cottage favourite. Gloves on when gathering!
ingredients.true_fact: During the First World War, Germany made army clothing from nettle fibre when cotton ran short.

ingredients.season: Leaves in early spring; roots lifted in autumn

culpeper.heading: DANDELION, VULGARLY CALLED PISS-A-BEDS.
culpeper.quote: the French and Dutch so often eat them in the Spring
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed dandelion, under Jupiter, had an opening and cleansing quality, and praised the French and Dutch for eating it in spring.

folklore.text: Children blew on dandelion seed clocks, counting the puffs needed to clear every seed to tell the hour. Roasted, ground roots were brewed as a coffee substitute.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: NCCIH says there is no compelling scientific evidence for dandelion for any health condition; very little research exists, mostly laboratory studies.

ingredients.safety: Likely safe in food amounts. May trigger allergies, especially with eczema. Possible interactions with diabetes, blood-thinning and water-pill medicines.
ingredients.card: Blow a dandelion clock and count the puffs: folk said the number told the hour. Its roots, roasted and ground, made a homely coffee, and its spring leaves were eaten as greens.
ingredients.true_fact: 'Dandelion' comes from the French dent de lion, 'lion's tooth', after its jagged leaves.

ingredients.season: Flowers in June and July; roots lifted in autumn

culpeper.heading: GARDEN VALERIAN.
culpeper.quote: The root smells more strong than either leaf or flower
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed garden valerian, under Mercury, had a warming faculty and helped coughs and shortness of breath. His plant may have been a related species.

folklore.text: Cats roll in bruised valerian, and rat-catchers baited traps with it. One old suggestion holds that the Pied Piper of Hamelin carried valerian root to lure the rats.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: NCCIH says evidence on valerian for sleep is inconsistent; sleep medicine experts recommend against it for chronic insomnia, and there is too little evidence for other uses.

ingredients.safety: Sedating: never combine with alcohol or sedatives. Can cause headache, dullness, vivid dreams; rare liver injury reported. Pregnancy safety unknown.
ingredients.card: Valerian's root smells so strong the ancients called it 'phu'. Cats adore it, and legend whispers that the Pied Piper kept some in his pocket to charm the rats.
ingredients.true_fact: Cats are attracted to valerian root and will roll on bruised plants.

ingredients.season: Early autumn: Culpeper says the heads are gathered in September

culpeper.heading: HOPS.
culpeper.quote: the heads are not gathered until the middle or latter end of September
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed hops, under Mars, opened obstructions of the liver and spleen and cleansed the blood.

folklore.text: Old English ale was brewed without hops. In 1530 Henry VIII's household rules told his ale brewer at Eltham to use no hops, but his beer brewer used them, and hopped beer won out in the end. The popular story of a nationwide ban is a myth.
folklore.source: Martyn Cornell, beer historian, 'Myth two: hops were forbidden by Henry VI and Henry VIII', Zythophile

science.text: EU regulators (EMA) accept hops only as a traditional herbal product for mild stress and sleep; trials mixed hops with valerian, so hops' own effect is unproven.

ingredients.safety: Sedating: may impair driving. Not advised in pregnancy, breastfeeding or under 12. Toxic to dogs (ASPCA).
ingredients.card: Pliny said the hop strangles willows as a wolf does a sheep; its name lupulus comes from lupus, 'wolf'. Henry VIII told his own ale brewer to keep hops out of the royal ale.
ingredients.true_fact: The hops brewers use are the papery cones of the female hop vine.

ingredients.season: Bulbs lifted in mid to late summer

culpeper.heading: GARLICK.
culpeper.quote: This was anciently accounted the poor man’s treacle
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed garlic, owned by Mars, was an old cure-all against venom and plague, though he admitted its smell made it offensive.

folklore.text: Herodotus wrote that an inscription on the Great Pyramid recorded how much was spent on radishes, onions and skorodon for its builders. Macaulay translates skorodon as leeks; most translators read it as garlic.
folklore.source: Herodotus, Histories, Book 2, ch. 125 (tr. G. C. Macaulay, public domain)

science.text: NCCIH says garlic supplements may lower cholesterol, blood pressure and blood sugar slightly; there is very little research on immune claims.

ingredients.safety: Supplements may raise bleeding risk, especially with blood thinners or before surgery. Raw garlic on skin can burn.
ingredients.card: Country folk called garlic 'the poor man's treacle': a homely standby for those who couldn't pay the apothecary. A braid hung by the hearth keeps for months.
ingredients.true_fact: 'Garlic' comes from Old English words for 'spear' and 'plant', after its spear-shaped leaves.

ingredients.season: Late summer, when it flowers

culpeper.heading: MUGWORT.
culpeper.quote: of a dark green colour on the upper side, and very hoary white underneath
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed mugwort, an herb of Venus, was chiefly an herb for women's complaints.

folklore.text: Before hops, mugwort flavoured beer. Medieval folk wore crowns of it on St John's Eve against evil, and believed it guarded travellers from weariness, sunstroke and wild beasts.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

science.text: NCCIH says very little research has been done on mugwort in people; there is not enough evidence to say whether it is safe or useful for any condition.

ingredients.safety: Must not be used in pregnancy. Safety otherwise unknown. Pollen is a common allergen, cross-reacting with fennel.
ingredients.card: Medieval travellers trusted mugwort to keep them from weariness on the road, and on St John's Eve folk wore crowns of it. In this shop it is sewn into pillows only, never brewed for drinking.
ingredients.true_fact: Before hops became common, mugwort was used to flavour beer.

ingredients.season: Spring: Culpeper says it is found only in April and May

culpeper.heading: MOONWORT.
culpeper.quote: Moonwort is an herb which (they say) will open locks, and unshoe such horses as tread upon it
culpeper.summary: Culpeper believed moonwort, owned by the Moon, healed wounds. He also reported, half-amused, that country folk called it 'Unshoe the Horse'.

folklore.text: Moonwort was thought magical if picked by moonlight, and Parkinson wrote that alchemists believed it could turn quicksilver into pure silver.
folklore.source: Mrs. M. Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), botanical.com

ingredients.safety: Not food or medicine. A small, easily overlooked fern that has declined across lowland Britain: look, never pick.
ingredients.card: A tiny fern with half-moon leaves, said to open locks and pull the shoes off passing horses. It is rare and fragile, so it lives only on our lore shelf: admired, never picked or brewed.
ingredients.true_fact: Moonwort is a fern, not a flowering plant; its 'flower' spike bears spores.
